business.title: Modeling the binding of fused pyrazole inhibitors to p38α MAP kinase using CorrEA-guided ensemble docking
business.desc: Mitogen-activated protein kinase p38α is an established therapeutic target implicated in inflammatory signaling and a variety of human diseases, including autoimmune disorders, cancer, and neurodegenerative conditions. Fused pyrazoles constitute an important family of ATP-competitive p38α inhibitors, displaying considerable structural diversity and a wide range of inhibitory activities. However, accurately describing inhibitor recognition remains challenging because the ATP-binding site of p38α is inherently flexible and cannot be fully represented by a single receptor conformation. Here, we constructed structural models for a series of 50 fused pyrazole inhibitors, comprising 1H-pyrazolo[3,4-b]pyridin-6(7H)-one (PPO) and 1H-pyrazolo[3,4-d]pyridazine (PPz) derivatives, by combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, ensemble docking, and the CorrEA methodology. Representative receptor conformations extracted from MD trajectories were used in cross-docking calculations, and the experimental potencies of the series were then supplied to CorrEA as selection criteria to retain, for each inhibitor, a single receptor–ligand complex from among the available docking solutions. The resulting models were examined through ligand pose comparisons, interaction fingerprint analysis, and characterization of conformational changes within the binding site. The ensemble model successfully described all inhibitors while preserving the canonical interaction pattern of ATP-competitive protein kinase inhibitors, revealing that subtle rearrangements of multiple binding-site residues collectively account for the observed differences in inhibitory potency. These findings illustrate how explicit incorporation of receptor flexibility improves the structural interpretation of structure–activity relationships and provide a practical strategy for modeling ligand recognition in flexible protein targets.

world.title: AMECEA: New Book Explores How SCCs Shape Mission, Family Ministry, and Youth Formation in Eastern Africa
world.desc:
Sr. Jecinter Antoinette Okoth, FSSA
Small Christian Communities (SCCs) have become the engine of missionary outreach, family and marriage ministry, and youth formation in the Catholic Church in Eastern Africa, according to a new four-volume work by Maryknoll Missionary Fr. Joseph Graham Healey.
The new book, titled Small Christian Communities in Eastern Africa: History and Evaluation, traces SCCs in the nine countries of the Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa (AMECEA): Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, South Sudan, Sudan, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia, and covers the period from 1961 to 2026.
Across 20 chapters and some 2,130 pages, the book, which was launched on Friday, 16 October 2026, at the Maryknoll Society's headquarters in Ossining, New York, measures the communities' growth in numbers and in quality, tracks the rise of young people, and examines their place in a Synodal Church in Africa.
Addressing participants who were present at the launch in person and those following virtually, the book's author, Fr. Healey, said the book had taken him 30 years to write, gathering stories from Maryknoll missionaries and countless Africans. With this vast outreach, the cleric emphasized, This is our book; it's not my book.
“Today there are 195,000 SCCs in Eastern Africa,” the member of the Maryknoll Mission Society disclosed, describing the SCCs as the church in the neighbourhood. He explained further that, “In rural areas, they are families living in the same section of a village; in towns, they are neighbours sharing apartment complexes.”
After 52 years of service in Africa, Fr. Healey said young adults have been among his greatest teachers, and the book devotes more than 200 pages to youth SCCs.
He stressed that the whole experience of SCCs is walking together, and emphasized the Spanish saying that runs through the book: se hace camino al andar, we create the path by walking.
On his part, Mr. Alloys Mogere Nyakundi, a Kenyan Catholic layperson who was present at the launch of the book in New York, offered living proof of the book's message.
He joined Kenyatta University in Nairobi, Kenya, in 2013 and graduated in 2017, during the long years when Maryknoll missionaries served as the university's Catholic chaplains.
The campus then had seven SCCs: one for lecturers and staff, several for residence students, and one for non-resident students. Each week members read and reflected on the coming Sunday's Gospel, but Nyakundi said the communities went well beyond Bible sharing.
It's through small Christian communities that we were able to understand the needs of different students, he said, noting that some students went a whole day without a meal. With this, every community held at least one charitable activity a semester, visiting orphans and prisoners, planting trees and reaching out to the marginalised.
He said the communities also answered a deep need for belonging among lonely students, and nurtured leaders. Seminarians and priests emerged from the Kenyatta University SCCs, and one former member is now a Member of Parliament in Kenya. The communities, he added, taught students to be truly synodal by giving them space to speak openly about their lives and to accompany one another.
Today, Mr. Nyakundi coordinates an online young adult SCC that links young people in the United States, Pakistan, Indonesia, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. Members use social media to evangelise one another and learn across cultures, then carry their faith into climate and social justice projects at home, such as tree planting.
The new book is a resource that will be used over the years on SCCs in the AMECEA region. As the Catholic University of Eastern Africa (CUEA) intends to introduce a degree in SCCs, the book is expected to serve as a key text for this new degree programme
The four volumes, each about 450 to 500 pages, are available on Amazon in hardback, paperback, ebook and audiobook. The audiobook runs to more than 100 hours.
